detail-body.a_greenhouse_monitoring_scenario_require: A greenhouse requires monitoring temperature, ambient humidity, light, and soil moisture, along with irrigation and ventilation actions. Historical analysis also requires defined schemas, quality checks, and reproducible data persistence.
detail-body.the_original_iot_project_used_sensors_es: The project began with the design and implementation of a greenhouse monitoring and control architecture as part of IoT studies (UTN, 2023–2024). I subsequently developed a data processing layer using Python and PySpark. The two phases share a domain and data model, but an automatic, continuous connection from the original physical system to the pipeline has not been established.
detail-body.connected_the_iot_architecture_around_te: I designed the IoT architecture with DHT22, TSL2561, and capacitive soil-moisture sensors, ESP32, Raspberry Pi, MQTT/Mosquitto, Node-RED, and Blynk, with irrigation and ventilation actuators.
detail-body.defined_datasets_for_sensor_and_actuator: I modeled devices, zones, sensor and actuator events, and prepared simulated data and external historical weather information.
detail-body.implemented_explicit_schemas_separated_r: I implemented Python/PySpark Bronze → Silver batch pipelines with explicit schemas, separate readers and writers, and dataset-specific quality checks.
detail-body.persisted_validated_analytical_data_in_p: I persisted validated records to Parquet, added execution/error logging, and documented the modules and processing sequences.
detail-body.from_sensor_signal_to_trustworthy_analyt: From sensor signal to trustworthy analytical record: the project connects physical systems with data engineering.
detail-body.the_repository_provides_evidence_of_modu: The project combines an understanding of IoT hardware and communications with data modeling, PySpark processing, data-quality validation, logging, and modular software design. It demonstrates a technical progression from physical monitoring to preparing structured datasets for analysis.
detail-body.the_public_repository_documents_a_bronze: The repository documents a Python/PySpark Bronze → Silver pipeline with previously verified execution and Parquet outputs. Its demonstration uses simulated sensor and actuator events, device/zone catalogs, and external historical weather information. The architecture builds conceptually on the earlier IoT system, but a continuous automatic connection between physical devices and the data pipeline has not been verified. The Gold layer and derived analytical indicators remain potential extensions. This is an academic and technical-portfolio project, not a commercially deployed system.

detail-hero.exploring_how_predictive_analytics_can_h: Data Science and Machine Learning project developed as part of the FaMAF–UNC diploma program, focused on identifying potentially fraudulent transactions through the preparation and training of a selected predictive model.

general.classification_methods_interpreted_throu: Classification methods interpreted through business risk

detail-body.fraud_detection_is_a_classification_prob:
Detecting potential credit card fraud presents a particular challenge: fraudulent transactions constitute a minority class, which makes them difficult to identify using conventional classification methods.
The objective was to analyze the patterns present in the data and develop predictive models capable of identifying potentially fraudulent transactions, while evaluating their performance in the face of class imbalance.
detail-body.the_group_worked_with_a_dataset_of:
As part of a diploma program offered by the Faculty of Mathematics, Astronomy, and Physics (FaMAF) at the National University of Córdoba—a program **recognized for its academic rigor and the depth of its training in programming, mathematics, statistics, econometrics, machine learning, and big data analysis**—I spent a year developing a credit card fraud prevention project.
The program was under the academic direction of Dr. Francisco Tamarit, **a leading Argentine authority on research into neural networks and machine learning**.
The project was based on a dataset containing 1,000,000 records and eight columns, for which I applied in-depth techniques in exploratory data analysis, predictive modeling, and model optimization.
detail-body.explored_distributions_anomalies_and_rel: I explored distributions, correlations, and transactional patterns, paying particular attention to class imbalance.
detail-body.worked_with_preprocessing_and_approaches: I organized preprocessing within pipelines and compared unweighted, class-weighted, and training-only undersampling approaches.
detail-body.compared_classification_approaches_and_s: I compared Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, and Random Forest, selecting hyperparameters with cross-validated Average Precision.
detail-body.interpreted_how_different_model_errors_w: I selected the decision threshold using F2 on a separate calibration set and documented false positives and false negatives on 200,000 held-out simulated transactions.
detail-body.in_fraud_analytics_evaluating_the_conseq: In fraud analytics, evaluating the consequences of a mistake is as important as measuring predictive performance.
detail-body.this_project_demonstrates_familiarity_wi: This project demonstrates exploratory analysis, supervised classification, cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, and reproducible evaluation. It also demonstrates my ability to critically review earlier work, correct methodology, and communicate applicability limits.
detail-body.the_four_recovered_notebooks_remain_hist: The 2026 reassessment used a public simulated dataset of 1,000,000 records. On 200,000 held-out transactions, the model detected 17,476 of 17,481 simulated fraud cases (99.9714% recall), with five false negatives and no false positives. The model was frozen before final testing. These results do not measure performance on real banking transactions or imply deployment. The original 2022 results are kept separate.
